era: Owner of the First House of Islam
teaser: He owned a house at as-Safa. He handed the key to the Prophet ﷺ, and it became the first school of Islam.
quran_mention: In houses which Allah has ordered to be raised and His name remembered in them — Quran 24:36

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: A young Makhzumi with a house at as-Safa
layers.content:
Al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam ibn Asad ibn Umar ibn Makhzum. His father's given name was Abd Manaf. His mother was Umayma bint al-Harith of Khuza'a, and his uncle Nafi ibn Abd al-Harith al-Khuza'i would later serve as Umar ibn al-Khattab's governor in Makka. His kunya was Abu Abdullah.

Banu Makhzum was not a weak clan. It was one of the heaviest names in Quraysh, and its men were among the fiercest opponents of the new call. That matters, because it means al-Arqam had something to lose. He was not a slave with no protector. He was a Makhzumi with standing, and he risked all of it early.

His grandson Uthman ibn al-Arqam used to introduce himself with a single line: 'I am the son of the seventh person in Islam. My father was the seventh to become Muslim.' Ibn Sa'd records it from him through his own family chain.

He owned a house at as-Safa, in the heart of Makka, within sight of the Ka'bah. In a city of a few thousand people, that address was not a hiding place. It was the most watched ground in Arabia.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: Seventh to believe, first to open a door
layers.content:
He came to Islam in the very first handful. His family transmitted the count plainly: the seventh.

What he did with that faith is what set him apart. Most of the early Muslims had only themselves to give. Al-Arqam had property, and he gave the property.

Al-Mubarakpuri summarises the situation of the fourth year of prophethood. The harassment had begun. The Prophet ﷺ advised his followers to conceal their conversion in word and deed, and to meet him in secret so that Quraysh would not learn his plans and move to break the young community while it was still fragile. He needed a room. Al-Arqam offered his.

So the Prophet ﷺ took Dar al-Arqam, the estate of al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam al-Makhzumi on as-Safa, as the place to meet his followers privately and instruct them in the Qur'an and in wisdom.

Think about the arithmetic of that offer. If the house were raided, al-Arqam would not be a bystander. He would be the host, from the clan of the persecutors, sheltering the man his own kinsmen wanted silenced.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 24:36 — «فِي بُيُوتٍ أَذِنَ اللَّهُ أَن تُرْفَعَ وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا اسْمُهُ» — 'In houses which Allah has ordered to be raised and His name to be remembered in them'
layers.source: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (The House of al-Arqam); Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: The room where the ummah learned to read
layers.content:
The house had a name of its own. Ibn Sa'd records that it was called the House of Islam.

What happened in it was teaching. Not politics, not planning — instruction in the Qur'an and in wisdom, delivered by the Prophet ﷺ to men who had to arrive one at a time and leave separately. Mus'ab ibn Umayr heard that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was calling people to Islam in the house of al-Arqam, went to him there, and accepted. Tulayb ibn Umayr became Muslim in that house and walked straight out to tell his mother. Ammar ibn Yasir met Suhayb ibn Sinan at its door — each of them alone, each too cautious to say why he had come, until one admitted he wanted to hear Muhammad speak and the other said, that is what I want too. They went in together and came out Muslim, concealing it until evening.

One night in that house the Prophet ﷺ made a supplication: 'O Allah, make Islam mighty by the one of two men You most love: Umar ibn al-Khattab or Amr ibn Hisham.' Umar ibn al-Khattab came the following morning and became Muslim in the house of al-Arqam. Then they walked out of it, said the takbir, and made tawaf of the House openly.
layers.hadith_ref: The supplication of the Prophet ﷺ in Dar al-Arqam, reported from Uthman ibn al-Arqam — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: He tried to protect it forever. He could not.
layers.content:
Al-Arqam knew what his house had been, and he tried to place it beyond the reach of money. He gave it as sadaqa to his son. Ibn Sa'd says a descendant read out the wording of the deed: 'In the Name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful. This is what al-Arqam has decided regarding his property at as-Safa: sacred in its site in the Haram, not to be sold and not to be inherited.' Hisham ibn al-As and a client of his witnessed it.

For generations it held. His children lived in it and traded from it.

Then the Abbasid caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur wanted it. A descendant, Abdullah ibn Uthman ibn al-Arqam, was already in prison in irons — an old man of about eighty. A man was sent to him with an offer: sell the house and perhaps your chains come off. He answered, 'It is sadaqa. But my right in it is his.' He signed his share away for seventeen thousand dinars. His brothers were then tempted with wealth and they sold too.

The first school of Islam passed into the hands of caliphs and their households, and was built over.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: How historians learned to date a man's faith
layers.content:
Al-Arqam did not stop at lending a room. He was present at Badr, at Uhud, at the Ditch, and at all the battles with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who tied him in brotherhood to Abu Talha Zayd ibn Sahl of the Ansar.

He died in Madina in 55 AH, about eighty years old. He had left an instruction: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas should pray over him. Sa'd was out at his fortress in al-Aqiq and slow to arrive. Marwan ibn al-Hakam, the governor, grew impatient — 'Is the Companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ held back for an absent man?' — and moved to lead the prayer himself. Al-Arqam's son refused him. Banu Makhzum stood with the son. Words were exchanged. Then Sa'd arrived and prayed over him, as al-Arqam had asked.

His strangest legacy is a phrase. Read Ibn Sa'd's biographies of the earliest Muslims and the same sentence keeps recurring: he became Muslim before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered the house of al-Arqam. A man's place in the first generation was measured against the day one door opened.

Al-Arqam gave a building. The ummah kept a calendar.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

quiz.prompt: What was al-Arqam's house at as-Safa used for in the early Makkan years?

options.text: A treasury for the wealth of the Muslims
A place where the Prophet ﷺ met his followers secretly and taught them the Qur'an
A hospital for those wounded in the persecution
A store for goods traded with Abyssinia

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, 'The House of al-Arqam'
quiz.scholar_reflection: The first institution of Islam was not a mosque or a court. It was a classroom in a private home. Before the ummah had a building, it had a lesson.

quiz.prompt: According to his own family, where did al-Arqam stand in the order of those who accepted Islam?

options.text: The third
The seventh
The fortieth
The last of the Makkan converts

quiz.citation: Uthman ibn al-Arqam, reported through his family chain in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: His grandson introduced himself as 'the son of the seventh person in Islam.' Some families inherit money. This one inherited a number.

quiz.prompt: Which future caliph accepted Islam inside the house of al-Arqam, the morning after the Prophet ﷺ supplicated for him there?

options.text: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
Uthman ibn Affan
Umar ibn al-Khattab
Ali ibn Abi Talib

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III, from Uthman ibn al-Arqam
quiz.scholar_reflection: The dua named two men and asked for either. One of them came through the door the next morning; the other became Abu Jahl. The same supplication carried both possibilities.

quiz.prompt: What did al-Arqam do with the house to protect it after his lifetime?

options.text: He sold it and gave the money away
He made it sadaqa in a written deed, not to be sold and not to be inherited
He gave it to the treasury of Madina
He had it demolished so no one could claim it

quiz.citation: The text of al-Arqam's deed of sadaqa, read out by a descendant — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He wrote the house out of the market and into the hands of Allah. Generations later a caliph still found a way to buy it. Intentions are recorded even when endowments are not kept.

quiz.prompt: Ibn Sa'd repeatedly dates an early Muslim's conversion by one event. Which?

options.text: Whether it was before or after the first migration to Abyssinia
Whether it was before or after the Prophet ﷺ entered the house of al-Arqam
Whether it was before or after the death of Abu Talib
Whether it was before or after the boycott of Banu Hashim

quiz.citation: Recurring dating formula in the biographies of the Muhajirun — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ubayda ibn al-Harith, Khabbab, Amir ibn Fuhayra and others are all placed 'before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered the house of al-Arqam.' One man's front door became the ummah's earliest timestamp.

quiz.prompt: Al-Arqam's contribution was a place, not a speech. What do you actually have that a community around you could use?
quiz.slider_label: Willingness to lend what you own

options.text: Space — a room, a table, a car, somewhere people can gather
Time, which is the thing I find hardest to give away
Skill — something I know how to do that others need
Honestly, I have not looked. I assume I have nothing worth offering.

quiz.citation: Reflection on Dar al-Arqam as the first gathering place of Islam
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was not asked to preach. He was asked for a room. The request that comes to you may be smaller and stranger than the one you were preparing for.

quiz.prompt: His own clan, Banu Makhzum, was among the fiercest opponents of the call. He hosted it anyway. What is hardest about standing apart from your own people?
quiz.slider_label: Cost of breaking with your own

options.text: The loss of belonging — you become a stranger where you were known
The suspicion that you might be the one who is wrong
Watching people you love treat you as a betrayal
Nothing about it is hard once you are certain

quiz.citation: Reflection on al-Arqam's position within Banu Makhzum
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not leave his clan; he stayed inside it and quietly worked against its project. That is a lonelier position than open exile.

quiz.prompt: The house was made an endowment so it could never be sold, and centuries later it was sold anyway. How do you hold a good intention that outlives your control?
quiz.slider_label: Trust in outcomes you cannot control

options.text: The reward was recorded when the deed was written, not when it was kept
You do the strongest thing you can and release the rest
It is genuinely painful, and pretending otherwise is dishonest
What lasted was never the building

quiz.citation: Reflection on the fate of the sadaqa of al-Arqam — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The stones passed to Khayzuran and her sons and then to others. The name of the house is still the name of a man who lent it. Ownership moved; attribution did not.

quiz.prompt: Ammar and Suhayb stood at his door separately, each afraid to say why he had come. Have you ever nearly turned back from something good out of caution?

options.text: Yes — and what got me through was finding someone else already standing there
Yes, and I did turn back, and I still think about it
I go in but I stay guarded for a long time afterwards
Caution at the door is not cowardice. It is how you survive.

quiz.citation: Ammar ibn Yasir's account of meeting Suhayb at the door of Dar al-Arqam — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Two men, both hesitating, each assuming he was the only one. The whole conversation was four sentences long. Then they went in.

quiz.prompt: Islam's first institution was a house where people learned to read the Qur'an. What does that suggest about where renewal starts?
quiz.slider_label: Where you expect change to begin

options.text: In small rooms, with a few people, before anyone is watching
In learning first — action without understanding does not hold
In someone deciding to be responsible for a space
In secrecy, because a fragile thing needs cover before it needs an audience

quiz.citation: Reflection on Dar al-Arqam as the first school of Islam
quiz.scholar_reflection: It was called the House of Islam while Islam was still perhaps forty people. The name was not describing what it was. It was describing what it would become.
